passage:
In Mrs Whitby's Year 5 class in Leeds, Nkechi could draw maps from memory and knew every capital in Africa. But whenever Mrs Whitby said, "Nkechi, would you—", her shoulders jumped up to her ears and she stared at her desk.
At break her friend Hana asked, "Is it because of the assembly? When your notes fell and everyone laughed?"
Nkechi frowned. "What assembly?" She truly seemed not to know. "I just don't like being picked."
Hana let it go. But she noticed Nkechi also went pale whenever the hall doors opened for Friday assembly.

qa.q: What happened at the assembly, according to Hana?
qa.a: Nkechi's notes fell and everyone laughed.

qa.q: Why does Nkechi tense up when Mrs Whitby calls on her if she can't remember the assembly?
qa.a: The embarrassment seems to have been pushed out of her memory, but the feeling is still there, so being picked makes her tense without her knowing why.

qa.q: What could Mrs Whitby try so that Nkechi feels safer being called on?
qa.a: Mrs Whitby could give Nkechi a quiet heads-up before asking, or let her answer in a small group first, so speaking up feels safe again.

qa.q: How might Hana feel after Nkechi says 'What assembly?'
qa.a: Hana may feel puzzled and a little worried, since she remembers the moment clearly and can see her friend flinch.

grounding: A nine-year-old cannot recall being laughed at in assembly, yet freezes whenever her teacher calls on her.

passage:
"Yash, can you come and solve this one?"
In the Class 5 room of a Kota school, Yash's pencil rolled off his desk. He bent for it and took a long time coming up. "Ma'am, can I go to the washroom?"
Rashmi Ma'am had seen this three times this month. At lunch she sat beside him in the empty classroom. "Is it about the Independence Day assembly? When your voice cracked in the song?"
Yash looked blank. "Was I singing?" He wasn't joking; he really couldn't place it. Then he rubbed his palms on his shorts, again and again.
"Okay," she said. "Next time, I'll ask you to tell me the answer from your seat first."

qa.q: What did Yash ask when he was called to the board?
qa.a: "Ma'am, can I go to the washroom?"

qa.q: What do Yash's palms rubbing on his shorts suggest?
qa.a: Even though Yash can't recall the assembly, his body still seems to hold the embarrassment, so the mention makes him nervous.

qa.q: What change did Rashmi Ma'am choose, and why might it help?
qa.a: Letting Yash answer from his seat first lowers the spotlight, so he can rebuild confidence before facing the class at the board.

qa.q: How might Yash's classmates read his trips to the washroom?
qa.a: They may think he's dodging work, without knowing that being called up seems to set off an old embarrassment he can't even remember.

grounding: A ten-year-old who cannot place the assembly where his voice cracked still slips away whenever the teacher calls him up.

passage:
My sister Kalyani is eleven and loud at home: she sings, argues, does all the voices. So what happened at her school prize day was strange. When her class teacher called, "Kalyani, come and read the vote of thanks," she went stiff and whispered that she had a headache.
Last year, at an assembly, she forgot her lines and a few boys laughed. I was there. When I mentioned it on the way home, she said, "That never happened. I've never read in assembly." I don't think she was lying. She just doesn't have it.
I can't know what's going on in her head. But she goes quiet every time a teacher says her name in front of people.
— Arnab

qa.q: What did the class teacher ask Kalyani to read?
qa.a: The vote of thanks.

qa.q: Why might Kalyani insist she has never read in assembly?
qa.a: The memory of being laughed at may have been pushed out of her mind because it hurt too much, while the fear still shows whenever she's called on.

qa.q: What could Arnab do with what he has noticed?
qa.a: Arnab could quietly tell a parent or the class teacher that Kalyani goes stiff when called in public, so an adult can help her feel safe again without forcing the memory.

qa.q: What is it like for Arnab to remember something Kalyani says never happened?
qa.a: Arnab is left unsure what to do, certain of what was seen yet not wanting to push a sister who genuinely seems not to remember.

grounding: A sibling notices an eleven-year-old who cannot recall being laughed at in assembly still freezing when a teacher calls her name.

passage:
Monday: In Class 6, Aadhya's teacher said, "Aadhya, come and read the poem." Aadhya's shoulders jumped, her face went pale, and she said she had a headache.
Wednesday: Her friend Tanmay asked, "Remember in Class 4, at assembly, when your skirt caught on the mic stand and everyone laughed?" Aadhya frowned. "That never happened. I don't remember that at all." She wasn't pretending; her face was blank.
Next Monday: The teacher called her name again, just to collect notebooks. Aadhya flinched as if someone had shouted, knocked her water bottle over, and stared at her desk. Later, walking home, she said to Tanmay, "I don't know why I hate being called up. I just do." Tanmay said nothing about the assembly this time.

qa.q: What did Tanmay say caught on the mic stand?
qa.a: Aadhya's skirt, at assembly in Class 4.

qa.q: Why did Aadhya flinch when the teacher only wanted notebooks?
qa.a: Aadhya felt a jolt of fear and embarrassment at being called up in front of the class, even though the assembly memory itself seemed gone from her mind.

qa.q: What could a teacher do if they noticed Aadhya's reaction to being called?
qa.a: They could speak with her privately and kindly, and give her small, safe chances to come forward, without mentioning the old incident in front of others.

qa.q: How might Tanmay feel after Aadhya said she didn't remember the assembly at all?
qa.a: Tanmay was probably puzzled and a little worried, which may be why Tanmay didn't bring it up again later.

grounding: Across several days, a girl cannot recall being laughed at in assembly, yet flinches whenever the teacher calls on her.

passage: Kunal, come, sit with your Bhavna Nani. You asked why I never speak at the family puja. Let me tell you. When I was nine, in Lucknow, I sang at school assembly and my voice broke on the high note. The whole hall laughed, even the teachers. For years, beta, I did not remember that day at all. If you'd asked me, I'd have said nothing happened. But every time a teacher said "Bhavna, stand up," my stomach dropped and my hands went cold. I didn't know why. I would say I had a cough. Only when I was thirty did my sister say, "Remember the assembly song?" and suddenly I saw the hall, the faces, all of it. The feeling had been steering me the whole time. So if something makes you freeze, Kunal, tell me. We'll find out why together.

qa.q: How old was Bhavna Nani when her voice broke at assembly?
qa.a: She was nine.

qa.q: Why did Bhavna Nani's stomach drop when a teacher said "Bhavna, stand up"?
qa.a: The humiliation from the assembly was still attached to being called up, even though she couldn't remember the day itself.

qa.q: What is Bhavna Nani offering Kunal, and why might it help?
qa.a: She offers to help Kunal find out why something makes Kunal freeze, so a hidden feeling doesn't steer Kunal unnoticed.

qa.q: How might Bhavna Nani's sister have felt seeing her face when she mentioned the assembly song?
qa.a: Her sister may have been surprised and sorry, realising that a day she remembered as a small moment had stayed so heavy for Bhavna.

grounding: An elder recalls forgetting the day she was laughed at in assembly while still freezing whenever called on.
